title: Med Spa Aftercare Instructions: What to Send and When (October 2026)
summary: Med spa aftercare instructions that patients actually read: what to include, when to send pre- and post-care messages, and how to automate them.
body_markdown:
## What Should Med Spa Aftercare Instructions Include?


A complete set tells the patient what to expect, what to avoid, what to do at home, when to come back, and which symptoms need a call. Anything beyond those five things is usually noise, and noise is why patients stop reading. The test is whether a patient who reads only the first three lines still avoids the most common mistake.


Most published guides agree on the same building blocks. Vendor guides from[Zenoti](https://www.zenoti.com/thecheckin/medspa-post-treatment-follow-up) and[Pabau](https://pabau.com/blog/automated-pre-and-aftercare-emails/) describe instructions written once per service and sent on a schedule. They are also candid that the clinical content is yours to supply, and the Zenoti guide leaves its aftercare details as placeholders for the medical team. That is the part you have to get right yourself:


- **What is normal:** redness, swelling, tenderness or bruising, and roughly how long each lasts for this treatment
- **What to avoid:** heat, exercise, alcohol, makeup, sun, active skincare, blood thinners, with a duration for each
- **What to do:** cleansing, sunscreen, cold compresses, sleeping position, products to use
- **Next steps:** the follow-up or maintenance visit, with a way to book it
- **When to call:** the symptoms that are not normal, and the number to call, including after hours


Write durations as numbers, not as "avoid for a while." A patient cannot follow "a while." Your medical director owns every one of those numbers, because they differ by product, device and patient.


## When Should You Send Pre-Care and Post-Care Instructions?


Send pre-care at booking and again shortly before the visit, send post-care the same day as the treatment, and add a single check-in a few days afterward. The reasoning is practical: pre-care only works if the patient has time to act on it, and post-care only works if it arrives while the treatment is fresh in their mind.


Message Send when Job it does


Pre-care, first send At booking Gives the patient time to stop products, arrange transport or skip the gym


Pre-care, reminder One to two days before Repeats the two or three rules that cause cancelled or compromised visits


Post-care Same day, after the visit is marked complete Covers what is normal, what to avoid, and who to call


Check-in A few days later Catches problems early and prompts any touch-up question


Maintenance prompt Near the expected rebooking window Turns the last visit into the next one


Zenoti's guide proposes five automated stages running from the day of treatment out to weeks six through eight. You do not need five. A provider who recently asked us how to send pre- and post-care instructions at all is better served by pre-care, post-care and one check-in done reliably than by a long sequence nobody maintains. Add the maintenance prompt once the first three work. Our guide to[med spa retention and rebooking](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-retention-and-rebooking) covers the rebooking window by treatment.


Trigger on the appointment, not on a person. If a staff member has to remember to send pre-care, some patients will not get it. The same logic applies to forms, which is why our post on[med spa consent forms](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-consent-forms) recommends sending them at booking.


## What Should Each Treatment's Instructions Cover?


Each service needs its own set, because the restrictions and the warning signs are different. A single generic sheet will be wrong for most treatments, and wrong in the direction that causes harm: either too lax for a device treatment or alarming for a routine injectable. The table lists what each set should address, not the clinical numbers, which your medical director supplies.


Treatment Pre-care should cover Post-care should cover Call-now symptoms to name


Neurotoxin Blood thinners and supplements, recent illness, event timing Lying flat, rubbing the area, exercise, heat, when results appear Drooping, trouble swallowing or breathing, vision changes


Filler Blood thinners, dental work, cold-sore history, event timing Swelling and bruising course, pressure on the area, sleep position, heat Vision changes, severe pain, skin turning pale, blue or dusky, spreading swelling


Energy devices and lasers Sun exposure, tanning, retinoids, active skin conditions Redness course, sunscreen, no picking, skincare restart date Blistering, signs of infection, burning that worsens


Peels and microneedling Active acids and retinoids, recent waxing or treatments Peeling course, gentle products only, sun avoidance Pain out of proportion, pus, fever


IV therapy Hydration, food, medication list, allergies Site care, what is normal at the insertion site Spreading redness, swelling, chest symptoms, rash


Weight-loss and hormone injections Storage and self-injection technique where relevant Side effects to expect, hydration and diet, dosing questions Severe abdominal pain, allergic reaction, symptoms your protocol names


The red-flag column is where specificity pays off most. The FDA's page on[dermal fillers](https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/aesthetic-cosmetic-devices/dermal-fillers-soft-tissue-fillers) identifies unintentional injection into a blood vessel as the most serious risk, with reported harms that include vision problems, stroke and tissue death. A patient who knows that pale or dusky skin and sudden vision changes mean calling immediately is a safer patient than one who was told to "contact us with any concerns."


## Which Channel Works Best: Text, Email, Portal or Paper?


Text gets read first, email holds the longer detail, and a portal page keeps a permanent copy, so the best setup sends a short text that links to the full instructions. Paper still has a place in the room, but it is the channel most likely to end up in a car footwell, which is why a paper-only clinic ends up fielding "can you resend that?" messages.


- **Text:** best for the two or three rules that matter most and for the call-now line. Keep it short.
- **Email:** best for the full instruction set, with photos or video if you have them.
- **Portal:** best as the permanent home, so the patient can find the instructions again next month.
- **Paper:** a useful backup in the room, never the only copy.


Treat the first message as a pointer, not a document. A text that says "Thanks for visiting today. Your aftercare is here: \[link\]. For anything urgent call \[number\]" gets used. A 400-word text gets skimmed. The setup work for the portal side is covered in our[patient portal setup guide](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-patient-portal-setup) .


## Is It Safe to Text and Email Aftercare Under HIPAA?


Yes, with reasonable safeguards. HHS states that HIPAA lets providers[use email to communicate with patients](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/faq/570/does-hipaa-permit-health-care-providers-to-use-email-to-discuss-health-issues-with-patients/index.html) when they apply reasonable safeguards, and that a patient who asks for a different channel should generally be accommodated. The same rule on confidential communications sits in[45 CFR 164.522(b)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/45/164.522) .


In practice that means three habits. Keep the message itself generic enough that a glance at a lock screen reveals little, put the detail behind a link, and record how each patient prefers to be contacted. Texting also brings its own consent and opt-out rules under the federal telemarketing regulations, summarized in[47 CFR 64.1200](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/47/64.1200) , so confirm with your attorney how your texts are classified and make sure a patient's "STOP" is honored. Our post on[med spa photo documentation under HIPAA and FTC rules](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-photo-documentation-hipaa-ftc) covers the neighboring question of what you may do with treatment photos.


## How Do You Handle a Patient Who Reports a Problem?


Route it to a clinician the same day, and decide the routing rule in writing before you need it. A front desk employee should never be the person deciding whether a swollen lip is normal. Aftercare messages invite replies, and some of those replies will be the worst moment of a patient's week.


1. **List trigger words.** Vision changes, severe pain, pale or dusky skin, trouble breathing, spreading swelling, fever.
2. **Name the on-call clinician** and their backup, with the number the patient should use after hours.
3. **Tell staff what to say.** "I am getting a clinician to call you right now," not a guess.
4. **Document everything** in the chart: the message, the time, who responded and what they advised.
5. **Review the event** if it was real, using the process in our guide to[adverse event reporting for med spas](https://decodahealth.com/blog/adverse-event-reporting-med-spa) .


The Zenoti guide, to its credit, builds a check-in stage into the sequence, but it never says where a worrying reply should go. That routing step is the gap between a nice message and a safe one.


## How Do You Keep Instructions Accurate Across Providers and Locations?


Give each service one owner and one current version, and send from that version only. Accuracy fails quietly: an injector changes a protocol, the handout stays the same, and two providers tell patients two different things. By the time someone notices, dozens of patients have received the old advice.


A practical routine is short. Keep every instruction set in one place, such as a shared library your team can search, with an owner, a last-reviewed date and the medical director's sign-off. Review the set whenever a product, device or protocol changes, and at least once a year. Our[guide to med spa staff SOPs](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-staff-sop-setup) shows how to structure that library so staff answer from it rather than from memory.


Multi-service visits need a rule too. If a patient has a peel and neurotoxin in the same appointment, decide which instructions go out, or whether they are combined into one message, and check how your software behaves. Some systems send only the primary service's sequence, so an add-on's restrictions can go missing. Test with a dummy booking before you trust it.


## What Do the Top Aftercare Guides Leave Out?


Most results for this search are written by software vendors or product retailers, and the same gaps repeat. They explain why aftercare matters, then stop short of the parts that make it work: the clinical wording, the routing of problem replies, and the upkeep of the library.


- **Clinical content.** Several guides ask your medical team to fill in the specifics and offer no examples, so owners are left with a framework and an empty template.
- **Escalation.** A check-in message is only useful if someone is ready to read the answer.
- **Consent and opt-out.** Texting rules get a sentence, or none.
- **Proof.** Pabau's page notes that sent instructions are logged in the client record, which is the part that matters if a patient later says nobody told them.
- **Maintenance.** No guide explains who updates the wording when the protocol changes.


If you fix those five things, your aftercare process is ahead of most of what ranks.

## Final Thoughts on Med Spa Aftercare Instructions


Start with your highest-volume service. Write its instructions in five parts, have your medical director sign off, and schedule three messages: pre-care at booking, post-care the same day, and one check-in a few days later. Send a test booking to your own phone before it goes live. Once that service runs without anyone remembering to send anything, copy the pattern to the next one.

## Frequently Asked Questions


What should med spa aftercare instructions include?


Good aftercare instructions state what is normal, what to avoid and for how long, what to do at home, when to book the next visit, and which symptoms mean the patient should call you or seek emergency care. Keep each set specific to one treatment and name a phone number that is answered. Your medical director should approve the wording for every service before it goes out.


When should you send pre-care and post-care instructions?


Send pre-care when the appointment is booked and again a day or two before the visit, so the patient has time to stop products or arrange their schedule. Send post-care the same day, ideally within a few hours of the visit, and follow with a check-in a few days later. The exact timing is a policy your medical director sets for each treatment.


Is it okay to text aftercare instructions to patients?


Yes, as long as the patient has agreed to be contacted that way and the message carries only what it needs to. HHS says providers may communicate with patients by email or text if they apply reasonable safeguards and honor a patient's request for a different channel. Keep clinical detail light, link to a secure page for longer instructions, and make sure opt-out replies are honored.


How do you make sure patients actually follow aftercare instructions?


You cannot guarantee it, but you can make instructions easy to find and hard to ignore. Send them as a short message rather than a PDF, repeat the one or two rules that matter most, and check in a few days later. Log what was sent in the chart so you can show the patient received the guidance if a complaint comes up.


Should aftercare instructions be different for each treatment?


Yes. Neurotoxin, filler, energy devices, peels, IV therapy and weight-loss injections each carry different restrictions and different warning signs, so one generic sheet will be wrong for most of them. Build one set per service, attach it to that service, and review the set whenever a product or protocol changes.


What should staff do when a patient reports a problem after treatment?


Route it to a clinician the same day. Staff should not diagnose by text. A written rule works best: any message mentioning vision changes, severe or worsening pain, skin that turns pale or dusky, trouble breathing or swelling that spreads goes straight to the provider on call, and the exchange is documented in the chart.
